title: Trie (prefix tree) explained: insert, search, autocomplete in Python — cv.cm
description: Learn how a trie (prefix tree) stores strings by shared prefixes: insert, search, starts-with and autocomplete in Python, with complexity and variants.
h1: Trie (prefix tree) explained: how it works, code and complexity
answer: A trie, or prefix tree, is a tree that stores strings character by character: each edge is a character, and each path from the root spells a prefix. Words that share a prefix share the same nodes, and a flag marks where a complete word ends. Inserting or looking up a word of length m takes O(m) time, independent of how many words are stored, and finding all words with a given prefix is fast. Tries power autocomplete, spell checkers and IP routing tables.

body: A hash set answers "is this exact word stored?" quickly, but it cannot answer "which stored words start with `pre`?" without checking every word. A sorted list can answer prefix queries with binary search, but inserts are slow. A trie is organized by prefixes, so prefix questions are its natural strength: autocomplete in a search box, word games, spell checking, and longest-prefix matching for network routes.

Think of a phone contact list that you narrow down one letter at a time. Typing `c` shows everyone starting with c, typing `ca` narrows the list, and so on. A trie stores the words in exactly that shape. The root is the empty prefix. Each node has a map from the next character to a child node, plus an end-of-word flag, because a word such as `car` can be both a complete word and a prefix of `cart`.

sections.h: Worked example: inserting car, cart, cat and dog
body: The four words have 13 letters in total but need only 8 nodes below the root (c, a, r, t, t, d, o, g), because `car`, `cart` and `cat` share `ca`. Searching for `ca` walks two nodes and succeeds as a prefix, but `ca` is not a word because its node is not marked as an end. Searching for `cow` fails at the second step: node c has no child o.
Each node holds a `dict` of children, which handles any alphabet including Unicode. The `starts_with` method collects every word below a prefix, which is the core of autocomplete.

body.code:
t = Trie()
for w in ["car", "cart", "cat", "dog"]:
    t.insert(w)
print(t.contains("car"), t.contains("ca"))  # True False
print(t.starts_with("ca"))                  # ['car', 'cart', 'cat']
print(t.starts_with("x"))                   # []

body: `starts_with` sorts its output for a stable order. A real autocomplete would also stop after the first few results and rank them, for example by stored popularity counts.

Time
Reason

body: The time does not depend on the number of words n, which is the main advantage over a balanced tree of strings (O(m log n) comparisons). The cost is memory: each node is a separate object with its own dictionary, so a trie can use many times more memory than the raw strings.

ul: Array children: use a fixed array of 26 slots for lowercase English. Faster than a `dict`, but wasteful for sparse or large alphabets.

Compressed trie (radix tree, Patricia trie): merges chains of single-child nodes into one edge labeled with a string, which saves a lot of memory. Radix trees are used for IP routing tables and in some HTTP routers.
Ternary search tree: each node has three children (less, equal, greater), which uses less memory than a wide array.
Counting trie: store a counter in each node to answer "how many words start with this prefix?" in O(m).
Bitwise trie: store numbers bit by bit to solve maximum-XOR problems.

body.note: The most common bug is forgetting the end-of-word flag. Without it, inserting `cart` makes `contains("car")` return True even though `car` was never inserted. A second common bug is deleting nodes that are still needed by longer words.

sections.h: When to use a trie and typical interview problems
body: Use a trie when you need prefix queries, longest-prefix matching or ordered iteration over many strings with shared prefixes. Use a `set` or `dict` when you only need exact-match lookups: it is simpler and uses less memory in Python. For small, static word lists, a sorted list with the `bisect` module also answers prefix queries well.

Typical problems: implement a trie (insert, search, starts-with), word search in a grid with many target words, replace words with their shortest root, longest common prefix, design a search autocomplete system, and maximum XOR of two numbers using a bitwise trie.

faq.q: Why is it called a trie?
faq.a: The name comes from the middle of the word retrieval. Edward Fredkin coined the term in a 1960 paper. Many people pronounce it like try to distinguish it from tree.

faq.q: Is a trie faster than a hash table?
faq.a: For exact lookups both take time proportional to the word length, and a Python `dict` is usually faster and smaller. A trie wins when you need prefix searches, sorted iteration or longest-prefix matching.

faq.q: How much memory does a trie use?
faq.a: In the worst case one node per stored character. Shared prefixes reduce this, and compressed tries (radix trees) reduce it further by merging single-child chains.

faq.q: What is the difference between a trie and a radix tree?
faq.a: A radix tree is a compressed trie: any chain of nodes with a single child is merged into one node whose edge holds a whole substring. The lookups work the same way but need fewer nodes.
